reason: §110 states the sun 'as gold and a heavenly body... contains an active sulphur of a red colour, hot and dry.' Quote exact, direction correct (Sol contains sulphur, not vice versa). Jung states this in his own expository voice, so jung-asserts is acceptable.

§110: Set/Typhon is 'the evil principle which, like the alchemical sulphur, is closely connected with the devil' — the 'like' presupposes and asserts sulphur's close connection with the devil. Quote exact; the devil-attribute aspect is genuinely asserted, not confused with sulphur's generative/luminous aspects.
§113: 'Hence there is also a Sol niger, a black sun, which coincides with the nigredo and putrefactio, the state of death.' Quote exact, direction and claim_type correct.

§116: 'the alchemical Sol, as a certain luminosity, is in many respects equal to the lumen naturae.' Ellipsis bridges only the parenthetical Latin; quote faithful. Jung's own conclusion ('we can say'), so jung-asserts fits. 'Corresponds-to' correctly softens 'in many respects equal.'

§117: 'Generally Sol is regarded as the masculine and active half of Mercurius.' Though phrased as the general view, Jung adopts and builds on it in his own analysis ('The ascending, active part of him is called Sol'), so jung-asserts is defensible. Direction correct: Mercurius is the supraordinate concept, Sol its half.
§117: 'The passive part therefore bears the name of Luna, because she borrows her light from the sun.' Quote exact, direction correct (Luna borrows from Sol).

§121: 'according to the arch authority, the Tabula smaragdina, Sol is the father of Mercurius.' Source and claim_type (jung-quotes-source) exactly right; direction correct for this stated aspect. The paragraph also reports the inverse ('Mercurius is the origin of Sol' per Exercitationes in Turbam) — that is a distinct, separately attributed aspect and does not undermine this edge.
§129: 'The refulgent body of the sun is the ego and its field of consciousness.' Quote exact; Jung's own psychological interpretation, jung-asserts correct.

§130: 'Among the significations of the sun as totality the most important was its frequent use as a God-image, not only in pagan times but in the sphere of Christianity as well.' Quote exact; Jung asserts this signification in his own voice.

§134: 'The close connection between them explains the view that sulphur was the companion of Luna.' Quote exact; explicitly a reported alchemical view ('the view that'), so jung-reports-parallel is the right claim_type.

§137: after quoting Dorn's De tenebris contra naturam, Jung writes 'Sulphur has here attained cosmic significance and is equated with the light of nature, the supreme source of knowledge.' Quote faithful, source Dorn correct, jung-reports-parallel correct for this reported Dornian designation.

§138: 'The strong body is the sun, as is clear from the saying: Sulphur blackens the sun and consumes it.' Quote exact; direction correct (sulphur consumes Sol). This destructive aspect is genuinely asserted alongside sulphur's generative aspect (§134 edge 10 context: Sol derives from sulphur) — both aspects are separately grounded, no conflation. Reported alchemical saying, so reports-type claim is right.

§140: 'Being the inner fire of Mercurius, Sulphur obviously partakes of his most dangerous and most evil nature.' Quote exact (footnote number ignored per rules); direction correct — sulphur is the inner fire of Mercurius, and the evil/dangerous aspect is asserted for exactly this relation.

§140: after listing Sulphur's epithets (artificer of a thousand things, heart of all things, begetter of every flower), Jung says 'This might well be a description of Eros' and then develops the interpretation seriously (Cupid imprisoned by Venus, concupiscence in Hermes Kyllenios). The mild hedge does not make 'corresponds-to' an overreach; jung-asserts is fair for Jung's own interpretive identification.

Content and quote are accurate — §143: 'for the alchemists sulphur was one of the many synonyms for the mysterious transformative substance.' But the text explicitly attributes the designation to the alchemists ('for the alchemists'), so this is a reported alchemical designation, not Jung's own assertion. claim_type jung-asserts is wrong.

§141 does state 'the dragon is clearly the filius macrocosmi and, as such, a parallel figure to Christ and at the same time his rival' — quote exact, direction fine. But Jung frames this as the alchemical/Gnostic analogy he is reporting ('Hence we get the parallel of the dragon's head with Christ, corresponding to the Gnostic view...'), a reported religio-historical parallel, not a direct Jungian assertion of identity. Christ/dragon parallels should be typed as reported analogies.

§145: 'This analogy shows that sulphur as the arcane substance was set on a par with Christ.' Quote exact; correctly typed jung-reports-parallel — Jung explicitly treats it as an analogy thrust on the alchemists by the unconscious, not his own theological claim. The 'as the arcane substance' aspect qualifier is preserved in the quote.

§172 quotes an alchemical source (footnote 270): 'Luna is the shadow of the sun, and with corruptible bodies she is consumed...' Quote exact across the ellipsis; direction correct (Luna is the shadow of Sol, consistent with §117 where Sol is the precious thing and its shadow res vilissima). jung-quotes-source is right; the source is footnoted but unnamed inline, so source:null is acceptable.

§175 does not flatly assert Sol symbolizes spirit; it invokes the equation conditionally as one alternative reading: 'Or, if Sol is the spirit and Luna the body, the spirit too may be corrupted by pride or concupiscence.' Jung is entertaining the traditional alchemical Sol=spirit/Luna=body attribution to make a point about corruption of spirit, not asserting the symbolism in his own voice here (his firm assertion in these chapters is Sol=consciousness, §116/§121/§129). Downgrade to a reported traditional attribution or re-anchor to a paragraph where the equation is asserted outright.
